anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'So saying, he drew his sharp sword... gathering himself together swooped like an eagle', directly before Achilles finds the fatal gap in Hector's armor.

anchors.anchor: Prone on the field the bleeding warrior lies,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'and goodly Achilles exulted over him', the taunt that opens this scene; Hector's dying plea for burial and Achilles's refusal follow within the same span, per the summary's fuller description.

anchors.anchor: Achilles, musing as he roll’d his eyes
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'He spake, and from the corpse drew forth his spear of bronze... set him to strip the... armour. And the other sons of the Achaeans ran up round about'; the nearest clean sentence-opening line just before Achilles's closing quip and the stripping of the corpse.

anchors.anchor: Now lost is all that formidable air;
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'So was his head all befouled with dust; but his mother tore her hair... and uttered a cry exceeding loud at sight of her son', directly preceding the parents' grief on the walls.

anchors.anchor: But not as yet the fatal news had spread
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'neither wist she anywise that... Athene had laid him low by the hand of Achilles. But the shrieks she heard...', opening the Andromache scene with her ignorance of Hector's death.

anchors.anchor: For such a warrior Thetis aids their woe,
anchors.note: Pope compresses the thrice-circling and the weeping-onto-the-sands into one quatrain (17-20) shared with scene 1; this is the next distinct line, matching Murray's 'so mighty a deviser of rout was he for whom they mourned', leading into Achilles's speech and vow.

anchors.anchor: And now a band of Argive monarchs brings
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the prince... was led unto goodly Agamemnon by the chiefs of the Achaeans', opening the scene at Agamemnon's tent.

anchors.anchor: He spoke: they hear him, and the word obey;
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'speedily making ready each man his meal they supped... they went each man to his hut to take his rest', immediately following Achilles's speech to Agamemnon.

anchors.anchor: But Agamemnon, as the rites demand,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the lord Agamemnon sent forth mules and men from all sides', directly after the ghost's parting words and the dawn.

anchors.anchor: The hero bids his martial troops appear
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Achilles straightway bade the war-loving Myrmidons gird them about with bronze, and yoke each man his horses'; the wood being cast down at the barrow site (Pope 164-167) is the compressed tail of the wood-fetching mission (n=108) rather than this scene's own opening.

anchors.anchor: Thus o’er Patroclus while the hero pray’d,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'He spake and set the lock in the hands of his dear comrade'; the cutting of the lock and the bulk of the Spercheius prayer belong to the prior scene's compressed span, so this is the nearest sentence-opening line to where Murray's text actually resumes.

anchors.anchor: Sad sacrifice! twelve Trojan captives fell.
anchors.note: Redrafted after verification: murrayOpening's first clause ('twelve valiant sons of the great-souled Trojans slew he with the bronze... and set the iron might of fire to range at large') is the killing of the twelve captives and the pyre catching fire, not the earlier host-dismissal; this line is the literal slaughter, immediately followed by the fire imagery ('the rage of fire victorious preys'), which precedes Achilles's address to Patroclus's ghost also contained in this scene's span.

anchors.anchor: So spake he, threatening: but the gods made vain
anchors.note: Matches Murray's opening about Aphrodite and Apollo protecting Hector's body; the sacrifice of animals and captives described in this scene's summary is rendered earlier, within the prior scene's compressed span.

anchors.anchor: “Not so (the dame replied), I haste to go
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'But Achilles prayeth the North Wind and the noisy West Wind to come... that so ye may rouse the pyre to burn', Iris's reply to the winds' invitation to feast.

anchors.anchor: So stay’d Achilles, circling round the shore,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'going heavily about the pyre with ceaseless groaning... even then grew the burning faint'; the preceding line ends a simile with a colon rather than a period, hence the expected warning.

anchors.anchor: That done, they bid the sepulchre aspire,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'they traced the compass of the barrow... and forthwith they piled the up-piled earth', directly followed by Achilles seating the host and producing prizes.

anchors.anchor: At once the coursers from the barrier bound;
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'they all at one moment lifted the lash... and sped swiftly over the plain'; Achilles posting Phoenix as judge (Murray's literal first clause) is rendered a couplet earlier.

anchors.anchor: Meantime the Grecians in a ring beheld
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the Argives sitting in the place of gathering were gazing at the horses... the first to mark them was Idomeneus'; Antilochus's reckless overtaking of Menelaus, named in this scene's summary, is rendered in the prior scene's span.

anchors.anchor: He said: Automedon at his command
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'placed it in Eumelus' hands and he received it gladly. Then among them uprose also Menelaus... wroth at Antilochus'; Nestor's prize and reminiscence, named in this scene's summary, are rendered later in the same span.

anchors.anchor: The prizes next are order’d to the field,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Then set he forth prizes for grievous boxing. A sturdy mule he brought and tethered', directly after Nestor's closing thanks.

anchors.anchor: The third bold game Achilles next demands,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the son of Peleus forthwith ordained... other prizes for a third contest, even for toilsome wrestling', opening the wrestling episode.

anchors.anchor: And now succeed the gifts ordain’d to grace
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the son of Peleus straightway set forth other prizes for fleetness of foot: a mixingbowl of silver', opening the footrace episode.

anchors.anchor: The effect succeeds the speech. Pelides cries,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'not in vain shall thy word of praise be spoken; nay, I will add to thy prize a half-talent of gold... the son of Peleus brought... a shield and helmet', the clean sentence-opening line just before Achilles's reply and the armor-duel prizes.

anchors.anchor: Then hurl’d the hero, thundering on the ground,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the son of Peleus set forth a mass of rough-cast iron, which of old the mighty strength of Eëtion was wont to hurl', the clean sentence start just after the sword prize is settled on Diomedes.

anchors.anchor: But when the tenth celestial morning broke,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'when at length the twelfth morn thereafter was come, then among the immortals spake Phoebus Apollo'; Pope gives 'tenth' rather than 'twelfth' but the moment and speech are unmistakable.

anchors.anchor: “If equal honours by the partial skies
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Then stirred to anger spake to him white-armed Hera: Even this might be as thou sayest... if indeed ye gods will vouchsafe like honour to Achilles and to Hector'.

anchors.anchor: He added not: and Iris from the skies,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'So spake he, and storm-footed Iris hasted to bear his message', directly after Zeus's instruction to fetch Thetis.

anchors.anchor: His word the silver-footed queen attends,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the goddess, silver-footed Thetis, failed not to hearken, but went darting down from the peaks of Olympus, and came to the hut of her son'.

anchors.anchor: While thus they communed, from the Olympian bowers
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'mother and son spake many winged words one to the other, but the son of Cronos sent forth Iris to sacred Ilios'.

anchors.anchor: She spoke, and vanish’d. Priam bids prepare
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'When she had thus spoken swift-footed Iris departed; but the king bade his sons make ready the running mule waggon'.

anchors.anchor: I go, ye gods! obedient to your call:
anchors.note: Matches Murray's declaration that he will go even at the cost of his life, immediately preceding 'He spake, and opened the goodly lids of chests... twelve beauteous robes'; Pope renders the whole outburst and the gift-gathering as one continuous sentence, so this is the nearest clean sentence start to where Murray's text resumes.

anchors.anchor: The sons their father’s wretched age revere,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'they, seized with fear of the rebuke of their father, brought forth the light-running waggon drawn of mules', directly after Priam's rebuke of his sons.

anchors.anchor: A dawn of joy in every face appears:
anchors.note: Matches Murray's account of the household's relief and the wagon setting out with Idaeus driving the mules and Priam his own horses; Pope renders the whole departure as one long sentence, so this is the nearest sentence-opening line to where Murray's text resumes.

anchors.anchor: Now twilight veil’d the glaring face of day,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'they halted the mules and the horses in the river to drink; for darkness was by now come down... Then the herald looked and was ware of Hermes hard at hand'; this scene's span runs on to include Hermes's full reassurance and offer to guide, per the summary.

anchors.anchor: He said, then took the chariot at a bound,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'leaping upon the chariot behind the horses quickly grasped in his hands the lash and reins... upon all of these the messenger Argeiphontes shed sleep'.

anchors.anchor: Thus having said, he vanish’d from his eyes,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'So spake Hermes, and departed unto high Olympus; and Priam leapt from his chariot to the ground', directly after Hermes's final instruction to entreat Achilles by his father.

anchors.anchor: Satiate at length with unavailing woes,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'when goodly Achilles had had his fill of lamenting... forthwith then he sprang from his seat, and raised the old man by his hand'.

anchors.anchor: To whom the king: “O favour’d of the skies!
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'And the old man, godlike Priam, answered him: Seat me not anywise upon a chair... nay, give him back with speed'; the 'two urns' speech that closes with 'thou mayst live to suffer more' belongs to the prior scene's span.

anchors.anchor: He said, and, entering, took his seat of state;
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'So spake goodly Achilles, and went back within the hut and on the richly-wrought chair... sate him down... and he spake unto Priam, saying: Thy son, old sire, is given back'.

anchors.anchor: Then gave his hand at parting, to prevent
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Achilles slept... by his side lay fair-cheeked Briseis. Now all the other gods and men... slumbered... but not upon the helper Hermes might sleep lay hold'.

anchors.anchor: Now shed Aurora round her saffron ray,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Dawn, the saffron-robed, was spreading over the face of all the earth. So they with moaning and wailing drave the horses to the city... Cassandra... marked her dear father'.

anchors.anchor: But godlike Priam from the chariot rose:
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the old man spoken amid the folk from out the car: Make me way for the mules to pass through... So spake he, and they stood apart'; the preceding line ends in a semicolon rather than a period, hence the expected warning.

anchors.anchor: But Priam check’d the torrent as it rose:
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the old man Priam spake among the folk, saying: Bring wood now, ye men of Troy'; the preceding line ends in a semicolon rather than a period, hence the expected warning.
